If the data being migrated into the SSD storage tier is being written faster than the rate at which the background tiering process can move it to the capacity pool tier, then the migration halts because FSx for ONTAP prioritizes front-end traffic over the background tiering task. You can choose from one of four tiering policies (by default, all volumes created with the AWS Console use the \u201cAuto\u201d tiering policy):\\\\n\\\\n+ Auto \u2013 Data is automatically transitioned to and from the capacity pool tier based on your access patterns.\\\\n+ Snapshot-only \u2013 Only data associated with previous versions of your files (i.e. data associated with a Snapshot of your volume) is transitioned to the capacity pool tier.\\\\n+ All \u2013 All data is transitioned to the capacity pool tier soon after it\u2019s written to the volume.\\\\n+ None \u2013 Tiering to capacity storage is disabled\\\\n\\\\nIf you\u2019ve selected a tiering policy of \u201cAuto\u201d or \u201cSnapshot-only\u201d, you can also optionally specify a minimum cooling period (between 2 and 183 days), which specifies how long a given portion of your data should have been inactive before it becomes a candidate to transition to capacity pool storage\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/fsx/netapp-ontap/faqs/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Migrating file shares to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP using AWS DataSync | AWS Storage Blog\",\"context\":\"## Get to know your volume data tiering policies\\\\n\\\\nAmazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP automatically transitions data between your system\u2019s SSD and capacity pool storage tiers, based on your data access patterns. With data tiering, you can achieve SSD levels of performance for your workload while paying for SSD storage for only a small fraction of your data. As a result, you need to provision primary SSD storage only for the active portion of your dataset, with the rest of your data stored in lower-cost capacity pool storage.\\\\n\\\\nEach volume in your Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system has a data tiering policy associated with it. You can choose from one of four tiering policies outlined in the FSx for NetApp ONTAP managing volumes documentation. In this post, I focus on the **Auto** and **All** policies for migrations.\\\\n\\\\n* **Auto** moves cold user data blocks in both the active file system and the snapshot copies to the storage pool tier. If read by sequential reads, such as those associated with index and antivirus scans, the cold data blocks stay cold and do not move to the primary storage tier.\\\\n* **All** moves cold user data blocks in both the snapshot copies and the active file system to the storage pool tier. If read, cold data blocks on the storage pool tier stay cold and are not written back to the primary storage tier.\\\\n\\\\nYou can set a specific cooling period for the Snapshot Only and Auto policies that range from 2\u2013183 days with a default of 2 days and 31, respectively\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/storage/migrating-file-shares-to-amazon-fsx-for-netapp-ontap-using-aws-datasync/\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. {"id": "55d92bf9-a3fb-4a5b-accc-e7b8084e4938", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Here's how storage tiering works on FSx for ONTAP volumes, and how I'd think about setting it up:

## The four tiering policies

Each volume gets one tiering policy that governs how data moves between SSD (primary) and capacity pool (lower-cost) storage:

- **Auto** (console default) — Moves cold *user data and snapshots* to capacity pool based on actual access patterns. Default cooling period is **31 days** (configurable 2–183 days). Best general-purpose choice: data that's read sequentially (e.g., antivirus/index scans) stays cold in the capacity tier, but randomly-read cold blocks warm back up to SSD.
- **Snapshot-only** — Only tiers data tied to Snapshot copies (not active file system data). Cooling period default is **2 days** (range 2–183). Good when your active dataset needs to stay fully on SSD but you want snapshot bloat moved off expensive storage.
- **All** — Tiers nearly everything (active + snapshot data) to capacity pool shortly after write, no cooling period to configure. This is also the policy required for Cloud Write mode. Good for archival/cold volumes or backup targets where you rarely need SSD-speed reads.
- **None** — Keeps everything on SSD, no tiering at all. Use for latency-sensitive, hot volumes where cost isn't the concern.

## How I'd approach setting it up

1. **Classify volumes by access pattern** — active production datasets vs. archival/backup vs. snapshot-heavy volumes.
2. **Default to Auto** for general workloads unless you have a specific reason not to.
3. **Use Snapshot-only** for volumes where primary data must stay hot but snapshot retention is long/large.
4. **Use All** for cold/archival volumes or if you're doing a Cloud Write migration.
5. **Tune the cooling period** — shorter cooling periods tier data faster (cheaper but risk re-tiering churn if data is briefly re-accessed); longer periods keep more on SSD (costs more but avoids tier flapping).
6. **Watch SSD fill rate** — if SSD exceeds ~98% utilization, capacity-pool tiering halts until space frees up, so leave headroom rather than running SSD near full.

If you'd like, I can pull up your actual FSx for ONTAP file system and volumes and suggest a tiering policy per volume based on their current configuration — want me to do that?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
